html:
Dhaka muslin was a very fine, light cotton cloth woven around Dhaka in Bengal, at its peak when Dhaka was the Mughal capital of Bengal from 1610 and in the 18th century.

It was spun by hand from a local cotton plant, phuti karpas, that grew along the Meghna river, and woven so thin that a length could pass through a ring. Mughal emperors and nobles wore it, and Bengal exported huge amounts through European companies. In late 18th century Europe muslin dresses became the height of fashion.

The trade collapsed in the 19th century. Machine cloth from Britain undercut it, a story told in the decline of Indian handlooms, and the craft and the cotton plant itself were lost. In the 2010s Bangladeshi researchers found the plant again and wove muslin once more. Dhaka still makes jamdani, a related patterned weave.
sum: Dhaka muslin was a very fine, light cotton cloth woven around Dhaka in Bengal, at its peak when Dhaka was the Mughal capital of Bengal from 1610 and in the 18th century.
